title: Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here’s Why That Doesn’t Add Up.
detail:
Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here’s Why That Doesn’t Add Up.
Jabran Kundi

AMZN

Walmart Inc. (NASDAQ:WMT) has opened a fulfillment center of more than 900,000 square feet in Stockton, California. The site uses automation and machine learning to cut the usual 12-step order process down to five. It will also employ about 1,000 people. The company says its next-generation fulfillment centers, of which Stockton is the fifth, will enable it to reach 95% of the U.S. population with next-day or two-day shipping when combined with the rest of its network. The stock closed more than 2% higher on October 8, its fourth straight gain. Beyond its push for faster delivery, Walmart's defensive appeal remains a key attraction for investors. But which other companies joined WMT on our list of the 10 Best Bear Market Stocks to Invest In Right Now?

Investors Are Paying More for Walmart Than Amazon. Here's Why That Doesn't Add Up.
Automation Is Changing Walmart's Business

I believe Stockton is just one piece of a much bigger shift. Walmart's U.S. e-commerce sales have grown more than 20% for 10 straight quarters, and fast deliveries jumped 48% last quarter. CFO John David Rainey said much of Walmart's recent spending has gone into supply chain automation and speed. That spending is also lifting higher-margin businesses. Advertising rose 38% last quarter, and membership fee revenue hit a record. Faster delivery brings more shoppers online, which feeds those businesses.

Still, Walmart remains a retailer at heart. Its stock fell 9% after its August report, despite beating estimates and raising its outlook. The decline reflected slow comparable sales and a soft Q3 guide, with operating income expected to grow just 2% to 4% as Walmart puts tariff refunds back into lower prices. Walmart's short-term margin pressure hasn't stopped hedge funds from backing the retail giant. See why WMT ranks No. 3 among the 10 Best Dividend Kings to Buy According to Hedge Funds and which other stocks made the list?

Walmart Costs More Than Amazon

Walmart's stock trades at a premium to its historical norms. The forward non-GAAP P/E of 37.48x sits about 24% above its 5-year average. That's even higher than Amazon, which trades at about 31x despite also owning AWS, a fast-growing, high-margin cloud business. The forward Price-to-sales ratio of 1.14x is also about 28% above its average. Yet analysts expect EPS to grow only 9% this fiscal year, about 12% in each of the next two, and 7% in fiscal 2030. Even based on fiscal 2030 earnings, the P/E would be around 28x. As of July 31, Walmart carried approximately $38.9 billion in net debt, excluding lease obligations. In my view, the automation story is big, but the stock already prices in a lot of it.

Consumer stocks were mixed late Tuesday afternoon with the State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLP) easing 0.1% and the State Street Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLY) gaining 0.2%.

In sector news, Redbook US same-store sales rose by 10.4% from a year earlier in the week ended Oct. 10 after an 8.6% year-over-year increase in the previous week. Ollie's Bargain Outlet (OLLI) shares rose 1.8% after the company said its board approved an additional $500 million share buyback authorization, bringing its total available buyback capacity to about $561 million.

Bumble (BMBL) shares surged 56% after it said Tuesday it has agreed to be acquired by Ithaca in an all-cash deal valuing the dating app at $1.3 billion.

Kroger (KR) plans to reduce more than one-third of its corporate workforce to simplify operations and improve competitiveness under new CEO Greg Foran, Bloomberg reported, citing a memo it reviewed. The company will cut about 3,000 roles across different functions over the next three years, the report said. Kroger shares were shedding 3%.

title: Should You Buy Target Stock For Its Cash?
detail:
Should You Buy Target Stock For Its Cash?
Trefis Team
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 8:49 AM MDT 4 min read
TGT
^GSPC
WMT
AMZN
COST
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Over the last twelve months, Target (TGT) generated free cash flow equal to 6.4% of its market value, against 4.4% for the median S&P 500 company. A cash yield sitting that far above the median signals one of two things: a fundamentally sound business priced cheaply, or a company investors expect to shrink. So what are you actually getting when you buy Target for its cash?

What You Own In Target's Cash

Buying shares means taking a stake in the free cash Target produces, regardless of whether the retailer pays it out. Cash retained inside the business still belongs to shareholders, exactly as profit does. Valuations typically adjust to reflect overlooked cash, particularly when that cash is growing.

Target pulls that cash from thin margins across 2,000 stores. Over the last twelve months, the retailer recorded a 5.6% operating margin, compared with 18.5% for the S&P 500 as a whole. Even with narrow margins, operations yielded $8.7 billion of cash in that period. The company directed about half of that total toward capital spending such as new stores and remodels, leaving $4.5 billion of free cash flow.

That cash generation has remained positive over the last three years, but the totals have fluctuated. Target posted positive free cash flow across all 13 rolling twelve-month periods during that time. The figure stood at $5.3 billion two years ago, dropped to $2.9 billion a year ago, and has since climbed back to $4.5 billion.

The retailer also carries more debt than cash, and creditors take priority over shareholders. Target holds $13.3 billion in net debt, a figure equal to 19% of its market value. Measured against market value plus that debt, the cash yield sits at 5.4%.

Questions like this one test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

Where Has Target's Business Been Weak?

Target recorded shrinking sales for two years, and the home and apparel categories remain persistent weak spots. The price appears to assume this weakness is not over. Twelve-month revenue declined 0.7% two years ago and fell 1.5% a year ago. During the latest fiscal year, sales of apparel and accessories dropped 4.7%, while home furnishings sales fell 6.5%.

Executives do not dispute the decline. During the August 19, 2026 call covering fiscal Q2 2026, management stated that performance in home and apparel "is not where it needs to be." They described growth in those segments as flattish, noting this is not the outcome they strive for, and they expect the repair work to run into 2027 and beyond. Target has also cut prices. The retailer lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in the twelve months before that call. On September 29, 2026, it reduced prices on nearly 2,000 additional home and apparel items.

title: Albertsons demands over $9bn from Kroger following merger collapse
detail:
Albertsons demands over $9bn from Kroger following merger collapse
The tie-up was halted by a federal judge in December 2024 after an intervention by the US Federal Trade Commission. Credit: Grossinger / Shutterstock.com · Retail Insight Network · Grossinger / Shutterstock.com

US supermarket group Albertsons has launched legal action demanding more than $9bn from Kroger following the collapse of the planned merger.

A two-week court hearing is set to start later this month to establish legal responsibility for the collapse of the $24.6bn buyout.

The planned acquisition would have united the two "largest" grocery operators in the US, according to Bloomberg, to rival Walmart and Amazon.

Albertsons claims that Kroger deliberately breached the contract by failing to make "best efforts" to obtain antitrust sign-off, pointing to an unwillingness to modify store sell-off arrangements.

Contractual stipulations obliged Kroger to resolve competition hurdles while capping store disposals at 650 outlets.

The damages Albertsons is pursuing exceed $9.3bn, covering deal premium payments designated for equity holders upon closing, a break fee of $600m, alongside $75m in costs and accumulated interest.

Albertsons said: "Kroger willfully breached these maximalist contractual commitments. Kroger wanted the merger but only on its own terms."

The firm added: "The bottom line is that Kroger made a promise and broke it. Kroger should be held accountable for the harm it caused our shareholders, associates, and customers – and we look forward to proving our case in court."

Kroger disputes any financial liability, contending that Albertsons neglected its own promises under the deal and forfeited any right to the termination payment.

It labelled Albertsons' wider financial demands a "far-fetched" concept centred on anticipated tax levies on the deal premium.

Maintaining that regulatory assent was impossible without exceeding the agreed 650-shop threshold, Kroger noted expenditure surpassing $1bn alongside "countless hours of personnel time in pursuit of the deal".

It additionally accused Albertsons of covertly partnering with prospective purchaser C&S Wholesale Grocers to demand further store sales.

Attorneys for Kroger argued: "Crediting Albertsons' endless second-guessing would convert the contractual control over regulatory strategy that is traditionally accorded to the acquiror into a guaranteed payout for the target company should regulatory efforts fall short".

The tie-up was halted by a federal judge in December 2024 after an intervention by the US Federal Trade Commission, which argued that offloading shops to C&S Wholesale Grocers failed to eliminate antitrust concerns.

Albertsons subsequently scrapped the pact.

"Albertsons demands over $9bn from Kroger following merger collapse" was originally created and published by Retail Insight Network, a GlobalData owned brand.
